transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-07-09 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Meeting ID: ff-20260709-tesserapay-01
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (TesseraPay CTO), Sara Nguyen (TesseraPay Head of ML), Priya Desai (TesseraPay SRE)
---
Summary: quick Optimize walkthrough focused on batching and prefix/K V cache cost tradeoffs; cost model live demo; next steps to run POC benchmark
---
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Uh we'll do a quick intros then jump into the Optimize walkthrough, focusing on batching and KV cache recommendations for your payments flows.
[00:18] Liam: Thanks Jordan. Quick context — we've got about 3k concurrent chats during peak, median prompt length around 120 tokens, but we've got some long flows up to 2,500 tokens. Our main concerns are latency under 400ms p50 and keeping hosting cost per thousand requests manageable.
[00:36] Maya: Got it. I, I pasted a short deck in the chat and a cost spreadsheet link — the spreadsheet has some scenarios I want to show.
[00:46] Priya: link? I didn't see it.
[00:48] Maya: ah yah, sending again — cost-model/redwood-tesserapay-2026 (shared drive).
[00:55] Sara: cool. Our architecture today is hybrid — some data in our V P C, and we can't send sensitive PII out of region. We'll need VPC/private considerations for the pilot.
[01:10] Jordan: Totally — Redwood Private and Dedicated options both support V P C and K M S integration, we'll put the SAML/SSO docs in the packet.
[01:22] Maya: Alright, jumping into batching first. There are two main approaches we recommend: request-level dynamic batching (runtime aggregates small requests into batches) and fixed-window batching (higher throughput but latency hit). For your latency target p50 400ms, dynamic batching with a 10-20ms aggregation window often hits better cost/latency sweet spot.
[01:46] Liam: can you quantify cost delta? like percent?
[01:50] Maya: yes — in the spreadsheet I have a scenario: with no batching baseline at your token distribution, cost per 1M tokens is $X (placeholder), enabling dynamic batching reduces that to about 65-75% depending on burstiness; fixed batching might push to 50% but increases tail latency to 700-900ms in some runs. (transcription note: numbers noisy in live voice)
[02:15] Sara: when you say dynamic batching, is that server-side only or is there a recommended client coalescing?
[02:20] Maya: server-side is easiest — Redwood's serving runtime does continuous batching. We do suggest small client-side hints for priority traffic (like auth flows) to skip batching. You can set per-route priorities.
[02:33] Priya: what about KV/prefix cache? We have a lot of repeated prompts at start-of-conversation — login, verification prompts — could we cache those?
[02:40] Maya: yes — there are two caching patterns to consider: prefix caching and key-value (K V) KV caching. Prefix caching is basically storing the computed key-value (KV) cache for a prefix — so we avoid re-computing the early tokens. KV cache is better when you have many sessions reusing the same context; it avoids re-encoding the prefix.
[02:58] Liam: is there a memory / cost tradeoff? if we cache tons of prefixes, we're paying for RAM.
[03:03] Maya: exactly. The cost model accounts for memory vs token compute. In practice, hit rates drive value — with hit rates above 30-40% for common prefixes caching pays off, because you avoid repeated attention computation and token generation cost. But if you cache low-frequency prefixes you pay for storage and eviction churn.
[03:21] Jordan: quick interjection — for your flows, if most users see the same login/consent chunks, that would be ideal for prefix caching. For personalized parts later in the conversation, KV cache helps a little but gets less re-use.
[03:33] Sara: how do you estimate hit rate? we have slightly personalized prompts so not all prefixes are identical.
[03:40] Maya: we usually derive a hit-rate from sampling logs — a 10k-sample of prompts and hashing prefix keys to estimate reuse. We'll run that for you during the POC.
[03:52] Liam: show us the cost model please.
[03:55] Maya: sure, opening the spreadsheet — slide 2 shows baseline. (pause, typing) so baseline no-batch, no-cache is row A: compute cost 100k units, network, infra — simplified. Row B adds dynamic batching: you see compute goes down 30%. Row C adds prefix cache with 45% hit rate: compute down 60% and effective cost per 1M requests reduces ~55%.
[04:25] Jordan: note these are model-agnostic assumptions but we'll also map to specific instance types in the pilot.
[04:30] Priya: are these numbers assuming quantized models or FP16? because our security team prefers known artifacts.
[04:36] Maya: great question. The cost model has toggles — default is quantized int8 path for cost calc. There's an alternate tab for fp16/amp where cost per token is higher. We'll include both in the sheet.
[04:48] Sara: any potential correctness regression with quantization + caching? like hallucination rates changing?
[04:53] Maya: caching won't change model outputs — it just reuses computation for tokens already computed. Quantization can have tiny differences; we recommend running quality evals over a held prompt set. Redwood Optimize has an eval hook to run regression checks and alert on quality drift — we'll enable that for the POC.
[05:10] Liam: latency — if we cache a prefix, does that add any extra lookup time? what's p50 impact?
[05:16] Maya: lookups are microseconds; the big wins are avoiding computation. Typical saved time per request can be 30-200ms depending on prefix length. For you that means improved p50 and especially p95.
[05:28] Jordan: I'll flag that caching usually improves both cost and tail latency if hit rate is decent.
[05:33] Maya: now showing the eviction policy options: LRU TTL-based evictions, or hot-key pinning for infinite TTL for small pinned prefixes. You can also configure global memory budget per ded- pool.
[05:46] Priya: how do we monitor hit-rate?
[05:49] Maya: Redwood Console has metrics per-route: cache_hits, cache_misses, hit_rate percentage, and average saved_tokens. We'll give you dashboard templates.
[05:59] Sara: what about consistency when models upgrade or you change tokenizers? will cached prefixes become invalid?
[06:05] Maya: yes — the cache keys incorporate model version, tokenizer hash, and prefix length. When you do a rollout, caches are invalidated or you can keep dual writes for compatibility during canary.
[06:18] Liam: do you support on-prem? we may want to run sensitive parts in our DC.
[06:22] Jordan: Redwood Private supports on-prem and V P C. For the POC we can run Dedicated in your region or spin up a private control plane; we'll scope it based on the pilot needs and timeline.
[06:33] Maya: jumping back to batching knobs — we showed aggregation window and max batch size. For conversational flows we often set max_batch_tokens so a single request doesn't blow up the batch. That avoids long waits for long sequences.
[06:48] Priya: what's a safe default?
[06:50] Maya: for you: aggregation 15ms, max_batch_tokens 8k, and route-level priority for auth flows to bypass batching. These defaults reduce token cost ~35% in our tests.
[07:04] Sara: you mentioned instrumentation earlier — can Redwood emit token-level cost attribution per request?
[07:09] Maya: yes, Redwood Console provides token_count, compute_ms, token_cost_estimate per request in logs and you can export to SIEM/billing system. That helps reconcile invoices.
[07:21] Liam: competitor question — do others do prefix caching?
[07:24] Jordan: some do but our integration with runtime batching + cache and the cost modeling is a differentiator. Others either do caching in-app or at a separate layer.
[07:33] (crosstalk)
[07:36] Maya: okay I'm going to run a short live demo of the spreadsheet scenario vs a small runner we prepared. I'll show a simulated workload of 1k sessions with a 45% shared-prefix hit rate.
[07:50] (typing, screen share noise)
[08:05] Maya: running baseline run now — you can see median latency and cost per 1k requests. Baseline median 380ms, cost X. Now enabling dynamic batching — rerunning. Latency p50 drops to 320ms, cost -30%.
[08:28] Sara: and now prefix cache?
[08:30] Maya: enabling prefix cache with pinning for top 50 prefixes — rerun. You can see p50 down to 280ms, p95 improved, and cost reduced further.
[08:45] Liam: interesting — is the prefix pinned in RAM? what's the per-prefix memory footprint?
[08:50] Maya: roughly proportional to KV cache tokens times model key-size; in the sheet we estimate 150-400KB per cached prefix depending on model size/kv layout. So 50 pinned prefixes might be 20MB-50MB — negligible on a dedicated GPU but matters for many thousands of prefixes.
[09:08] Priya: how do we size memory in Dedicated?
[09:11] Maya: we'll run a sample with your prompts during the POC and produce recommended instance/gpu SKU and pool sizing. In the optimize tab I included recommended SKUs for throughput targets.
[09:24] Sara: let's talk about edge cases — say user flows include small variations in phrasing, will fuzzy matching help for cache hits?
[09:32] Maya: we don't do fuzzy cache matching at runtime by default; it's strict key match. For fuzzy reuse we recommend prefix normalization or using hashed canonical prompts at generation time. We can help generate a prompt-normalization layer in the POC.
[09:46] Liam: security question — are cached prefixes encrypted at rest and in transit?
[09:50] Maya: yes, for Redwood Private and Dedicated we support encryption at rest via K M S keys and in transit via TLS. For hosted we have controls, and for Private you can bring your own K M S/HSM.
[10:02] Priya: ok good. Also need audit logs — who accessed cache?
[10:06] Jordan: Console provides audit logs and per-request trace id mapping into cache hits; we'll include a sample log output.
[10:15] Maya: moving on to the POC suggestion: 2-week pilot with three phases — sampling and hit-rate estimate (3 days), benching with 1k simulated sessions (7 days), integration and monitoring setup (rest). We'll produce a runbook and scripts.
[10:33] Sara: timeline sounds reasonable. We have sign-off from infra for a small Dedicated trial. Budget needs to be under $Xk for initial pilot — we'll confirm.
[10:42] Jordan: understood — we'll size the pilot to fit budget and show ROI via the cost model.
[10:46] (long pause, notes)
[11:00] Maya: quick note on rollouts: if you change model version we recommend canarying 10% traffic and keeping dual caches until stable. We can automate fallback to a lower-cost variant if tail latency or error rate spikes.
[11:16] Liam: ok. can Redwood instrument stimulus->response quality diff for the canary?
[11:20] Maya: yes, Optimize ties evaluations to prompt sets; we'll run BLEU/embedding-similar/regression checks and alert if similarity dips beyond threshold.
[11:30] Sara: sample integration question — our auth flow hits 2-3 external services before prompt. Will Redwood add significant extra latency?
[11:36] Jordan: Redwood's runtime is just the model serving piece — network hops are additive; we'll help you isolate where its contribution is. With caching you'll likely reduce total processing time.
[11:46] Priya: is throttling supported if we exceed quota?
[11:49] Maya: yes per-route rate limits, quotas, and graceful degradation policies — auto-fallbacks to smaller model variants one of them.
[11:58] Liam: any pitfalls you commonly see?
[12:01] Maya: common pitfalls — over-caching low-frequency prefixes, too-large batch windows raising p95, and not instrumenting hit-rate which leads to surprises. Also forget to invalidate caches on tokenizer or model changes.
[12:14] Sara: on the instrumentation we need log export to our splunk.
[12:18] Maya: supported — we have log sinks and can push to splunk/elk. I'll include config snippets.
[12:25] Jordan: alright quick recap — we'll send the sheet and slides, Maya will prepare the POC runbook and runner, TesseraPay to share sample prompts and confirm pilot budget & infra constraints.
[12:38] Liam: sounds good. Couple last quick q's — will you share expected SLA numbers for Dedicated?
[12:43] Jordan: yes SLA doc in the enterprise pack. We'll attach it.
[12:47] Sara: one more on billing — can we get per-route invoicing?
[12:50] Maya: yes you can tag routes and get per-route cost breakdowns in Console + billing export.
[12:57] Priya: thanks all, this was helpful.
[13:00] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up on the three action items.
---
Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (K V vs KV), numbers in the live demo are approximate and will be provided precisely in spreadsheet.
